That’s when I realized how much tension there was among some parents. Lost and worried, many wonder what the government is doing and are calling for intervention where they themselves seem no longer able to do anything. That’s how the idea for a report on the recruitment of youth came to me.
Dans le but de mettre en lumière un phén: In order to shed light on a phenomenon that, unfortunately, doesn’t seem to be going away, I tried to paint a realistic picture of the situation and of what emerged from the testimonies I gathered. What held me back the most is that this is an extremely sensitive subject, yes, but also a very complex one. We’re talking about people in very vulnerable situations: populations living in marginalized and often underfunded neighbourhoods, who get labelled and saddled with a bad reputation. We’re also talking about young people whose reality is completely new, since technology and social media have to be taken into account, and about parents who no longer know what to do to save them from delinquency and who come from a racialized community that already faces its share of challenges.

La tension est palpable à Montréal. Des: The tension in Montréal is palpable. Distraught parents, overwhelmed community workers, police services stretched thin: in recent years, more and more minors are making the headlines. Whether they are victims, offenders, involved or not, teenagers are being used as cannon fodder by older criminals, more hardened in the underworld.
Souvent comparés à des « enfants soldats: Often compared to “child soldiers,” these teenagers, who are getting younger and younger, are lured by promises of quick, easy money. That is what parents like Hocine*, who lost his son in an incident of gun violence, fear the most: that their children will lose their way, drawn in by the lure of profit. He also shares another fear: that young people, like his son, will become collateral victims of a phenomenon of disturbing scale.
Lui, ainsi que plusieurs autres parents,: He, along with several other parents, is demanding solutions: how far will the authorities let this ordeal go? Must there be more stories like that of <l1>Yanis Seghouani</l1>, the barely 14-year-old who died last September while going to provoke a biker clubhouse in Beauce; of <l2>Mehdi Moussaoui</l2>, who also died at 14 behind the wheel of a car in the middle of the night; or of <l3>Meriem Boundaoui</l3>, killed by a stray bullet in a vehicle? The parents gave up their jobs – he was a jurist and she a medical specialist – to offer a better future to their son and to their daughters, who would be born in Montréal.
« Nous vivions dans un petit coin de par: “We were living in a little corner of paradise,” recalls the man in his sixties. A few years after the family settled in Quebec, everything was going well: Hocine’s small medical business was running like clockwork, his wife had found a job in the pharmaceutical industry and his son was about to begin university studies. Everything was going well, until his son’s death.
Alors âgé de 19 ans, le fils aîné de Hoc: Hocine’s eldest son, then 19, was killed in a shooting in 2019. He was not the target. “I don’t want to dwell on the past and talk about my son’s death again, but I want people to know the pain I felt and that it was not eased in the slightest by the authorities,” he says quietly. “My son was cowardly murdered because he was in the wrong place at the wrong time.”
Il a fallu un an pour que les enquêteurs: It took a year for the investigators on the case to conclude that the young man had no record and had most likely been the collateral victim of an attempted murder. “A year to clear my son’s name,” Hocine says indignantly, adjusting his glasses on his nose. “A year before they considered his death serious.”
Aujourd’hui, Hocine est frustré. « J’ai: Today, Hocine is frustrated. “I always prayed that my son would be the last on an already long list. Unfortunately, there are even more victims of youth violence,” he says, shaken. His son’s death ultimately made him realize that the system he lives in could not provide him with the safety he is entitled to, he feels. “I’m a full citizen. I pay my taxes like everyone else; I also have a right to the safety I’m promised. And all the parents who have lost their children in these circumstances have that right too. The system failed, the system let us down,” he says bluntly.
Le sexagénaire pense qu’il n’y aura pas: The man in his sixties believes nothing will change until the authorities take real action. “The parents are not at fault, community organizations can’t do everything, the police can’t constantly watch over our youth,” he concludes. In his view, sounding the alarm to alert elected officials, who hold real legislative power, is the only way to change the dangerous path that some young people are taking.

He issued an urgent call for a “review of the laws against the practice of recruiting vulnerable youth by criminal groups.” “Offenders who,” he adds, “take advantage of young people’s vulnerability and exploit it must be punished more severely.”

Fontecilla n’est toutefois pas totale: Mr. Fontecilla is not entirely convinced by that approach, however. “We can consider increasing sentences for the perpetrators, but I don’t think that will solve the problem. Even if we make sentences heavier, there will still be crimes. Young people won’t be thinking about that,” he believes. “We might get results, but only in the very long term.” He is also aware that a good number of the criminals who send orders to the youngest are already behind bars.
S’il tente de convaincre le gouvernement: While he is trying to convince the government to explore the options citizens are asking for, he still believes it’s necessary to work upstream with law enforcement, already present on the ground. “The police are an integral part of the solution,” he does not hesitate to say. “But we mustn’t forget that their role is to repress crime. Offenders have to be locked up. However, I doubt that increasing police numbers will solve the problem,” he adds. “We have to work upstream with peace officers. All the actors around young people who are on the path to crime have to collaborate to properly support them,” he thinks.
Plus que tout, il croit que le gouvernem: More than anything, he believes the government is “being stubborn and turning a blind eye to an alarming situation,” he says.
Il est persuadé que, pour éviter que des: He is convinced that, to keep young people from taking the road to delinquency, intervention on the ground is one of the key solutions. “Beyond the measures the government has to take, we have to build a community around young people,” he says. “That happens through parents at home, school staff, community workers and police officers on the street, and so on. We have to create a web around the young person,” he concludes.
Dans un long courriel envoyé à La Conver: In a long email sent to La Converse, the Ministry of Public Security (MSP) says it is “very concerned about gun violence among young people.” “It monitors the evolution of crime, identifies vulnerability and protective factors, and anticipates new criminal trends,” the MSP’s media relations officer assured us in the email.
Afin d’assurer l’établissement d’un port: To ensure that a concrete picture of the situation is established, it says it is taking the necessary steps. “The <l1>Quebec strategy to combat gun violence</l1> (called CENTAURE) targets gangs in particular. Le MSP explique que les objectifs de la: The MSP explains that the objectives of the CENTAURE strategy are prevention, repression and knowledge development, and that 40% of the strategy’s funds are dedicated to youth prevention initiatives.
« En 2023-2024, 40,5 M$ ont été investis: “In 2023-2024, $40.5 million was invested to support 300 initiatives, mainly intended for community organizations to hire community workers and implement support measures for at-risk youth,” the email also states.
